title: Failure You Should Pay For
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: The Business Leader Daily takes aim at the gap between leaders publicly celebrating a "culture of failure" and actually building the specific conditions that make failure worth having. Drawing on Amy Edmondson's research, the piece argues that most leaders skip the parameters when they tell teams to stop fearing failure, when in fact an "intelligent failure" must clear four specific bars: it happens in genuinely new territory with no existing playbook, chases a goal worth chasing, is informed by prior homework, and is kept as small as possible while still teaching something real. The newsletter draws a sharp distinction between intelligent failures (worth celebrating), basic failures (preventable errors in familiar work), and complex failures (systemic pileups), arguing both of the latter deserve investigation rather than either applause or blame. It closes with a stack of quotations from Edmondson, Hill/Tedards/Wild, and Ryan Holiday reinforcing that failure tolerance is a designed condition, not a slogan.
points: The piece's central correction is that leaders who announce 'we should be comfortable with failure' without naming Edmondson's four conditions (new territory, worthy goal, prior homework, minimal scale) are giving teams permission with no usable parameters.

The three-way distinction between intelligent, basic, and complex failure gives leaders a diagnostic instead of a single blanket reaction: basic failures are preventable errors, complex failures are systemic pileups, and only genuinely novel, well-prepared, small-scale attempts qualify as 'intelligent.'

The Fearless Organization quote reframes the barrier to intelligent failure as a rational calculation, not a personality flaw: staying silent feels safe with certainty, while speaking up carries the uncertain payoff of actually changing the outcome.

Citing four different authors (Edmondson twice, Hill/Tedards/Wild, and Holiday) on the same theme signals that failure tolerance is being treated as a load-bearing leadership competency across multiple management traditions, not one writer's pet idea.
quotes: Failure is a popular idea and an unpopular practice. Leaders want the potential benefits without building what produces it.
A failure earns the word intelligent when it clears four bars. It happens in genuinely new territory where no proven playbook exists. It chases a goal worth chasing.

Basic failures are preventable errors in familiar work. Complex failures are the pileups that occur when several things go wrong at once within a system you thought you understood. Neither one deserves applause. Both deserve investigation.
The failure is intelligent because it's the result of a thoughtful experiment, not a haphazard or sloppy one, Amy C.
We can be completely confident that we'll be safe if we are silent, and we lack confidence that our voices will really make a difference, Edmondson writes elsewhere, in The Fearless Organization.
Every moment of failure, every moment or situation that we did not deliberately choose or control, presents this choice: Alive time. Dead time, writes Ryan Holiday in Ego Is the Enemy.
